szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial Intelligence Framework Integrates Urban Building Energy Modeling Across Life Cycles

A comprehensive review of urban building energy modeling methodologies shows how artificial intelligence is transforming city-scale energy simulations into an integrated framework spanning urban design, building renewal, and multi-building operations. In an analysis examining the progression of urban building energy modeling alongside conventional and advanced artificial intelligence paradigms, researchers Chao Wang, Xin Wang, Francesco Causone, and Xing Shi detailed the operational mechanisms, computational bottlenecks, and systematic literature trends governing city-scale decarbonization. Urban areas represent a critical juncture in the global climate crisis because they account for approximately seventy percent of global greenhouse gas emissions while experiencing a roughly seventy-four percent increase in heat-related mortality across the past three decades. To bridge analytical projections and practical physical interventions, the researchers formalized an extended paradigm termed UBEM plus, which expands standard urban building energy modeling across the key stages of design, renewal, and operational management to foster low-carbon, thermally comfortable urban environments.

Standard urban building energy modeling generates baseline predictions of city-scale building energy consumption and simulated indoor and outdoor environmental conditions to support strategic urban planning. The extended UBEM plus framework builds upon this foundation by establishing distinct computational workflows tailored to three specific stages of the built environment lifecycle. In the design phase, the framework focuses on optimizing urban form and building layouts to enhance microclimates and reduce overall energy demand, requiring design alternatives whose computational complexity scales with search spaces, evaluation frequencies, and model coupling. During the renewal phase, the system evaluates retrofit options and renewable resource availability across existing building stocks, with computational loads dictated by combinatorial intervention strategies and uncertainty analyses. In the operational phase, the framework integrates system diagnosis and control optimization to coordinate energy demand dynamically across multiple buildings, adjusting its processing burden according to prediction horizons, update frequencies, and required system response times.

Transitioning the extended framework from academic theory into widespread implementation is hindered by three core structural barriers identified in the review. First, the deeply interdisciplinary nature of urban modeling requires fusing heterogeneous data sources from building physics, meteorology, human behavior, socio-economics, and electrical engineering, all of which exhibit disparate formats, spatial and temporal resolutions, and granularities that complicate consistent evaluation. Second, scaling from individual properties to urban districts creates high-dimensional modeling obstacles, as vast variations in building geometry, construction materials, HVAC systems, and occupant schedules dramatically increase the parameter space. Detailed simulations capture this physical heterogeneity only at substantial computational expense, whereas simplified models risk sacrificing predictive accuracy. Third, urban environments constitute interconnected and dynamic cyber-physical-social systems where structural modifications, local microclimates, and regional energy grids continually interact and evolve over time, demanding modeling architectures capable of capturing longitudinal interdependencies.

To evaluate how researchers have historically addressed these modeling challenges, the authors executed a systematic literature retrieval across the Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect databases covering English-language publications from 2020 through a cutoff date of July 24, 2026. Applying standardized query combinations combining artificial intelligence terms with urban design, renewal, building energy, and operational control, the initial search retrieved 3,499 records. Following the removal of 1,074 duplicates and 49 ineligible document types, title and abstract screening excluded 281 records focused exclusively on single-building, indoor-environment, or component-level analyses. Further content relevance screening eliminated 1,367 studies concerning unrelated spatial, agricultural, or environmental domains, and a subsequent eligibility assessment removed 255 papers lacking building-demand integration or direct modeling links, resulting in a finalized thematic corpus of 473 publications. Geographical distribution revealed that China contributed the largest share with 185 publications, followed by the United States with 45, the United Kingdom with 22, South Korea with 21, Canada with 19, and Italy with 16, with general modeling representing 44.8 percent of the corpus, design accounting for 27.9 percent, operations comprising 15.0 percent, and renewal making up 12.3 percent.

Methodological analysis of urban building energy modeling indicates an evolutionary trajectory divided fundamentally into top-down and bottom-up paradigms. Top-down methodologies rely on aggregated historical energy statistics to construct macroeconomic relationships linked to gross domestic product and population, but they cannot assess targeted planning or physical retrofits. Conversely, bottom-up methodologies compute individual end-use energy demands and aggregate them to district or metropolitan scales, dividing into physics-based, data-driven, and hybrid modeling. Physics-based techniques, first formalized as a coherent three-part pipeline of data inputs, thermal modeling, and validation in 2016, rely on geometric, non-geometric, and weather data. While geometric data acquisition has accelerated through open databases, unmanned aerial vehicles, and advanced 3D spatial modeling, non-geometric data acquisition remains constrained by access barriers and behavioral uncertainty. To navigate these constraints, deterministic archetypes assign uniform parameters across building classes, though they fail to reflect real-world variation, whereas probabilistic forward methods use Monte Carlo sampling to propagate parameter distributions, and inverse calibration approaches iteratively refine prior distributions using Bayes’ theorem against measured utility consumption.

Microclimate inputs and model validation represent persistent technical challenges within physics-based simulations. Standard typical meteorological year files collected in rural or peripheral locations fail to capture urban heat island effects, prompting the deployment of observational monitoring stations, satellite Earth observations, and simulation-based climate modeling. Among numerical weather tools, computational fluid dynamics programs like CityFFD resolve micro-scale airflows and convective heat transfers within a five-kilometer radius at significant computational expense; meso-scale numerical weather prediction models such as the Weather Research and Forecasting platform operate up to two thousand kilometers but lack local building-scale turbulence resolution; and urban canopy models like the Urban Weather Generator strike a balance between accuracy and runtime across district areas up to fifteen kilometers. Validation remains similarly constrained by sparse access to sub-annual or building-specific metering, forcing widespread reliance on aggregated annual city records that mask underlying inaccuracies through balancing effects where positive and negative errors cancel out.

Data-driven modeling has transitioned rapidly from early statistical regressions to advanced machine learning and deep learning pipelines structured around data collection, feature selection, model training, and performance metrics such as mean squared error, root mean squared error, and R-squared.
